Andvari cursed it as he went into the rock: the gold would be the death of two brothers and the strife of eight princes, and no man should joy in his wealth. When the skin was covered, Hreiðmarr saw one whisker still showing, and Óðinn had to give up the ring to hide it. So the ransom that was meant to settle a killing carried a spoken curse into the house that received it. Reginsmál: The Patricide of Gnitaheiðr Fáfnir and Reginn demanded the blood-gold from their father as their share after Ótr. Hreiðmarr refused — and Fáfnir put his sword through his father sofanda , sleeping, while the old man called on his daughters to witness that his life was spent. Fáfnir took all the gold, and when Reginn asked for his inheritance, Fáfnir gave him a plain no. Then Fáfnir went out to Gnitaheiðr , the Gnita heath, and there his greed finished what the curse had begun: he took on the likeness of a serpent — var í orms líki , as Reginsmál puts it — and lay brooding on the gold, wearing the ægishjálmr , the helm of terror that all living things feared, and blowing poison across the land so that none dared come near. Reginn, the cunning smith, went to the court of King Hjálprekr and became foster-father to the young Sigurðr, son of Sigmundr — and began, patiently, to point the boy at his brother. Fáfnismál: The Strike from Beneath Reginn forged for Sigurðr the sword Gramr , so keen it sheared a lock of wool drifting down the Rhine and split Reginn's anvil in two. On the heath Sigurðr dug a deep trench in the dragon's track to the water and lay down in it; when Fáfnir crawled overhead, blowing venom, Sigurðr thrust Gramr upward into the heart. The dying dragon questioned his killer — Fáfnismál grants him a long, sardonic deathbed dialogue — and warned him twice: þér verða þeir baugar at bana , these rings will be your death. Reginn cut out the heart and set Sigurðr to roast it. Testing whether it was done, Sigurðr burned his thumb and thrust it into his mouth — and the moment the dragon's heart-blood touched his tongue, he understood the speech of birds. The nuthatches in the thicket told him Reginn meant to betray him and claim the gold alone; Sigurðr struck off Reginn's head, ate the heart, and loaded the hoard onto his horse Grani. He had won the treasure — and inherited the curse, which would ride with the gold to the hall of the Gjúkungs and bring down the whole Vǫlsung line. Syncretism: Fáfnir belongs to the common Germanic heroic stock rather than to any cult, and his closest kin are literary. The continental redaction of the same legend-complex survives in the Middle High German Nibelungenlied , where Siegfried slays a dragon and wins the hoard of the Nibelungs — though there the dragon and the curse have drifted apart, the hoard's doom attaching to the Burgundian kings instead. The Old English Beowulf offers the nearest analogue scene: a fire-dragon coiled for three hundred years on a barrow-hoard, roused by the theft of a single cup, slain by a hero it kills in turn. Comparison is often drawn with the Indo-European serpent-slaying myth — the storm-god's combat with a watery serpent — but Fáfnir is a different creature: not a chaos-monster opposed to cosmic order but a man whom avarice deformed, a moral dragon rather than a cosmic one. The Norse Þiðrekssaga preserves yet another redaction of the Reginn–Sigurðr material, and in later Scandinavian folk tradition the dragon on the gold-barrow became a standing figure of sterile, hoarded wealth. The line descends unbroken into modern fantasy: Tolkien's Smaug is openly the heir of Fáfnismál's talking, riddle-loving worm. Cultural legacy: Wagner fixed the dragon's modern image: in Siegfried , the third opera of the Ring des Nibelungen , the giant Fafner — who has already murdered his brother Fasolt for the ring — has used the Tarnhelm to become a dragon and sleeps on the hoard in a forest cave until Siegfried's sword Nothung finds his heart; tasting the blood, Wagner's Siegfried likewise comes to understand the Woodbird and, warned by it, kills the treacherous Mime. Wagner conflated Hreiðmarr's sons with the giant brothers of his own invention, but the kinslaying for gold and the blood-taught birdsong come straight from Reginsmál and Fáfnismál. Tolkien acknowledged Fáfnir among the chief models for Smaug — the speaking dragon on his gold, with the one unarmoured patch beneath. In comics, Marvel's Fafnir appears as a Thor antagonist, the monstrous king of Nastrond; in games the name surfaces from Final Fantasy to Smite and God of War , where Fáfnir is remembered as a dwarf whose greed turned him dragon. The idiom of the dragon-hoard — wealth kept and never used — is his permanent bequest to the language of moralists. In modern Heathenry Fáfnir is no object of cult but a cautionary emblem: the man who embraced gold until the embrace became scales. Extended meditation: Names are not merely labels; they are compressed worlds. Fáfnir — the embracer — names a man who embraced gold so completely that the embrace became his skin. The medieval scribes who wrote the name marked its long á with care, and the Unicode restoration keeps that mark: the length of the first syllable is the length of the boast he traded for a life. A dragon, in the end, is what a hoard does to the one who will not let it go. Original script note: The name is Old Norse Fáfnir , written in the Latin alphabet by the medieval Icelandic scribes of the Codex Regius and Vǫlsunga saga. A Viking-Age carver would have rendered it in the Younger Futhark — a plausible runic spelling is ᚠᛅᚠᚾᛁᚱ — and the sixteen-rune row of that period does not mark vowel length at all: the acute accent on á is the modern editorial normalization that records the long vowel which metre and grammar attest. The Unicode restoration Fáfnir keeps that mark. As a registrable domain the restoration becomes fáfnir.com, which IDNA encodes as the punycode xn--ffnir-xqa.com — the long á travelling intact through the machinery that plain ASCII would strip away.

Pronunciation of Hēraklēs: /hɛː.ra.klɛ̂ːs/ Label: Classical Attic Greek Reconstruction Approximation: "hay-RAH-KLAYS" — first syllable deeper and longer than English 'hay'; the final syllable is held and falls in pitch, like 'klays' sung on a descending note. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: Hē-: Rough breathing [h] plus long open-mid front eta [ɛː] — the 'Hera' element, sustained and deep. -ra-: Short alpha with rolling alveolar rho, the link between the two halves of the name. -klēs: Kappa-lambda followed by long eta with circumflex [klɛ̂ːs], carrying both length and the falling pitch accent. Note: Hēraklēs is Tier 1 because Classical Attic Ἡρακλῆς contains both length (long η in the first and final syllables) and stress (circumflex on the final -klēs). The registrable form Hēraklēs preserves length with macrons; the acute/circumflex is omitted because fully accented Greek letters are often untypeable and are not reliably registrable as IDN labels. Reconstruction follows Allen, Vox Graeca: The Pronunciation of Classical Greek, 3rd ed. (Cambridge, 1987); LSJ; and Beekes, Etymological Dictionary of Greek (Brill, 2010).
